title: The People's Revolution (1897)
content:
## The Revolution of 1897

On the fourteenth of March, 1897, workers at the Ashenmere textile mills staged a walkout that became, within seventy-two hours, a national uprising.

King Aldric IV had ruled a nation that was culturally rich and economically stagnant — a kingdom that had not industrialized, that taxed its poorest subjects most heavily, and that maintained its aristocracy's privileges through a combination of tradition and inertia. The treasury was empty. The harvest had failed two years running. The mills, which had expanded rapidly to meet export demand, had cut wages three times in eighteen months.

When the Ashenmere workers walked out, the King ordered the garrison to restore order. The garrison's officers refused. Several later said they could not see the difference between "order" and "shooting people for being hungry."

Aldric IV abdicated on the seventeenth of March. He was given safe passage to Lytheira, where he lived in comfortable exile until 1923.

## The First Constitution

The Constitutional Convention of 1897 produced a document remarkable for its time: universal male suffrage (women were not enfranchised until 1921), free press protections, parliamentary sovereignty, an independent judiciary. The First Republic lasted thirty-seven years — chaotic, corrupt in places, frequently ineffective, and genuinely, noisily free.

Halvek suspended the constitution in 1934. The argument about what that constitution was — and what it should become — has never been resolved. It is the argument Katerin Ashavel was elected to answer.

title: The Halvek Regime (1934–1960)
content:
## General Edvard Halvek

Halvek staged his coup on January 11th, 1934 — Veltria's coldest winter in recorded history. He called it a "correction." The banking crisis had produced 30% unemployment; three governments had collapsed in eight months; communists and nationalists fought in the streets of Ashenmere. Many people welcomed the tanks. This is not a comfortable fact, but it is a fact.

What followed was twenty-six years of what Halvek himself called "structured authority." He did not call it a dictatorship. He maintained a parliament — neutered, appointed, but present. He did not, technically, abolish the constitution — he simply extended its emergency powers indefinitely and concentrated them entirely in the Chancellorship.

## The Record

**Halvek's genuine achievements:** Kravenstal's steel industry — built. The national highway network — built. Mass literacy programs — completed. The infant mortality rate dropped by 60% in his first decade.

**Halvek's crimes:** The Bureau of National Integrity, which filed surveillance records on one in every twenty-three adult Veltrians. The "Silent Clearances" in Dravenhollow — the forced displacement of 40,000 Dravenni people from their ancestral lands. An estimated 4,000 political prisoners; the new government is still compiling the list. The execution of Mikhael Ashavel and hundreds like him for the crime of having opinions.

## The Death and Its Aftermath

Halvek died of a stroke on March 3rd, 1960. He left no named successor and no instructions. The three-year transition that followed was chaos — which is how Katerin Ashavel became Chancellor. Not because the system produced her, but because it briefly, exhaustedly, failed to prevent her.

title: Bureau of National Integrity (BNI)
content:
## The Bureau of National Integrity

Established by decree in 1936. Stated mandate: to protect the Republic from "subversive elements, foreign intelligence operations, and enemies of national unity."

Actual mandate, as operations documents recovered in 1963 confirm: to identify, monitor, neutralize, and where necessary eliminate political opposition.

## Scale and Method

At peak operation in the mid-1950s, the BNI employed **4,200 full-time agents** and an estimated 12,000–18,000 informants — recruited through a combination of ideology, financial incentive, and coercion. It maintained surveillance files on approximately 200,000 citizens. It intercepted mail, recorded telephone conversations, ran informants inside universities, churches, unions, and civil society organizations.

Its headquarters, a gray concrete building on Veltria Avenue in Ashenmere, was known informally as "The Silence" because no one who entered under arrest was heard from again for a long time, if at all.

## The Unresolved Question

When Halvek died, the BNI was not dissolved. When the transitional government failed to consolidate power, the BNI was not dissolved. When Katerin Ashavel was sworn in as Chancellor, surveillance operations were still ongoing — files dated four days after her inauguration confirm journalists and union organizers under active monitoring.

The BNI's intelligence on Tyvaren military movements is, according to some, the most current Veltria has. This creates a dilemma that has no clean resolution: the tool of oppression is also, sometimes, the tool of defense.

title: The Silence (1938)
content:
## The Silence

*From the personal accounts of Katerin Ashavel, recorded during her years in opposition.*

The country had learned to be quiet by 1938. The reading groups met underground now. Books that mattered passed hand to hand with the covers torn off, so a search would find nothing worth confiscating.

A wrong word in the wrong seminar and a student simply stopped attending. No one asked where he went. Everyone already knew not to ask.

## The Press Under Halvek

The press was nationalized entirely. The state decided what the people were allowed to know, and the punishment for the truth was exile or worse.

By 1938, every newspaper in Veltria carried the same headline each morning — whatever the Bureau of National Integrity had approved the night before. Independent radio was shut down. The few journalists who had resisted were either in prison or in exile, and their names could not be spoken aloud.

## Fear as Architecture

Fear became the ultimate enforcer. The state didn't need to arrest everyone; it only needed to make the silence deafening enough that no one dared to break it.

This was the world Katerin Ashavel grew up in — a world where the truth was contraband and silence was survival. She was nineteen years old, and she had already learned the most important lesson of her generation: that courage is not the absence of fear. It is the decision that something else matters more.

title: What They Took (1943)
content:
## What They Took

*From the personal accounts of Katerin Ashavel, recorded during her years in opposition.*

By 1943, the BNI had taken thousands. The pharmacist on one street. The teacher who vanished between the autumn term and the spring. Every family in the country had learned the sound of a car engine idling at night.

They didn't knock. They never needed to. The taking wasn't the point — the certainty that no one could stop it was the point.

## The Machinery of Disappearance

The state machinery consumed its own citizens, one street at a time. The infrastructure crumbled while the Party built monuments to itself.

The BNI operated without warrants, without trials, without public record. An arrest was not an arrest — it was a "protective interview," conducted at an undisclosed location. The detained were not prisoners — they were "guests of the state" undergoing "civic rehabilitation." The language was precise, clinical, designed to make the disappeared seem like they had never existed at all.

Families received no notification. There was no body to bury, no trial to attend, no lawyer to consult. One day a person was there; the next day they were not, and the neighbors had already learned to pretend they had never been.

## The Basement

The country was locked in a basement of its own making, and the door was guarded by fear.

Katerin Ashavel was twenty-four in 1943. She had already lost her father, Mikhael, to the regime. She would later say that the years between 1943 and 1951 were the years she spent learning to be angry without being consumed by it — years that taught her that rage, however justified, is not a strategy. Something harder was needed. Something more patient.

title: Those Who Came (1951)
content:
## Those Who Came

*From the personal accounts of Katerin Ashavel, recorded during her years in opposition.*

By 1951, ordinary people had run out of official doors to knock on. A widow with a petition no ministry would accept. Dockworkers whose union had been dissolved by decree. A schoolteacher wanting to know if the constitution still technically existed.

They climbed three flights of stairs to a rented office above a printer's shop, because someone had told them there was a lawyer there who actually listened.

## The Stairwell

The office was small — a desk, two chairs, a window that didn't close properly. Katerin Ashavel was thirty-two years old and had been practicing law for six years. She had no staff, no secretary, no filing system beyond a cardboard box under the desk.

She saw them anyway. Every one.

The dockworkers came first. Their union had been dissolved by decree in 1947, and they wanted to know if there was a legal path to reconstituting it. There wasn't — not under Halvek's emergency powers. But Ashavel spent three hours explaining why, and when they left, they did not leave defeated. They left informed. They left knowing that the law had been used against them, not that the law was inherently against them. The distinction mattered.

## The Seed

It was the dockworkers who said it first, out loud, the thing that had been building in that stairwell for months: the country needed someone who would not look away. They had started to believe that person was you.

Ashavel did not believe them at first. She was a lawyer, not a politician. She believed in documents, in arguments, in the slow machinery of legal precedent. But the people who climbed those stairs were not asking for legal precedent. They were asking for someone to stand in front of them and say: this is wrong, and I will not be quiet about it.

She would spend the next decade learning to say exactly that.
